title: Prefill thresholds vs timeout — postmortem and tuning notes
content:
Summary:

This doc summarizes the prefill-thresholds vs timeout experiment runs we did during Dec 2025–Feb 2026 and records a short postmortem of why a specific customer incident on 2026-01-22 surfaced severe p99s for size-1 single-turn requests. The goal was to understand if tunable prefill thresholds (prefilling KV cache / warm-up work) combined with timeouts produces better tail behavior and fairness than conservative timeout-only flush rules.

TL;DR findings:
- A small prefill threshold (0.15–0.25 of max-batch capacity) reduces p50 and p95 consistently for medium-length sequences by allowing earlier coalescing of warm requests, but it can hurt p99 for latency-sensitive tiny requests when prefill attempts cause head-of-line blocking under microbursts.
- Timeout-only strategies with very low timeouts (2–4 ms) keep tiny request p99 lower but reduce throughput and increase GPU kernel inefficiency (more small kernels, lower utilization).
- Dynamic prefill (aggressively prefill when queue age > X or when incoming rate shows low variance) recovers both latency and utilization in simulated steady bursts; however it requires robust starvation detection to avoid demotions that cause fairness violations.
- Root cause for 2026-01-22 incident: prefill threshold was set to 0.2 in prod on a mixed-tenant node; a microburst of small single-token chat pings coincided with a long-running conversational batch, and the prefill behavior pinned slots causing queue head-of-line blocking.

Experiment setup (replicable):
- Hardware: single A100-80GB equiv. instance (prod-like), identical kernel stack used in Dedicated pool.
- Model: Llama2-13B-chat quantized (fp16 execution path), typical max seq len=1024.
- Synthetic workload: mixed-size Poisson arrival process made of: 70% tiny requests (input tokens < 8), 20% medium (8–128), 10% long (>128). Peak RPS tuned to produce 70–90% GPU occupancy.
- Scheduler variants tested: timeout-only (T={2,4,8,16} ms), prefill-fixed (P={0.1,0.15,0.2,0.3} of batch capacity), prefill-dynamic (P_base=0.1 with age-/variance-driven boosts), and hybrid (prefill+soft-deadline flush).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency end-to-end, kernel utilization (% cycles at >50% occupancy), batch-size distribution (histogram), fairness (Jain's index computed over per-tenant avg latency), queue age distribution, KV-cache hit ratio, and tail amplification factor (p99/p95).

Key results (select numbers representative from runs):
- Timeout-only T=4ms: p50=9ms, p95=38ms, p99=110ms; GPU kernel utilization 62%; batch-size median=3, mean=3.6; throughput baseline 1.0x
- Prefill-fixed P=0.2, T=8ms: p50=7ms, p95=30ms, p99=160ms; GPU util 76%; median batch-size=6, mean=7.4; throughput 1.25x but p99 regressed by ~45% vs timeout-only
- Prefill-dynamic (age boost when queue_age>6ms): p50=8ms, p95=32ms, p99=95ms; GPU util 74%; fairness (Jain) improved relative to fixed prefill (0.88 vs 0.79); throughput 1.15x
- Hybrid (P=0.15 + soft-deadline flush at 40ms): p50=8ms, p95=28ms, p99=92ms; GPU util 71%; throughput 1.12x; best combined tail & throughput balance in mixed workloads

Observations and explanations:
1) Head-of-line blocking caused by prefilled batches
   - When a prefill batch is formed using pending warm requests, the scheduler pins a set of slots waiting for more arrivals (to reach a profitable kernel size). If a long-running request is included (or a multi-tenant heavy request), the pinned slots delay later tiny requests that would otherwise have been flushed quickly with a short timeout.
   - In practice we saw the pinned batch often contained 1–2 heavy requests that amplified p99 by 2–3x during microbursts.

2) Timeout costs to utilization tradeoff
   - Very aggressive timeouts (2–4ms) keep tiny-request latency low but fragment batches. This reduces kernel amortization and increases tail variance due to heterogeneous kernel overheads. For throughput-sensitive customers, tight timeouts increase cost per token by ~12–20%.

3) Dynamic prefill recovers tail when combined with age signals
   - The dynamic policy that boosts prefill aggressiveness only when the median queue age is low (system under steady load) avoided over-eager pinning during microbursts. This reduced p99 flare-ups without sacrificing too much utilization.

4) Fairness and tenant interference
   - Fixed prefill thresholds disadvantaged tenants issuing many tiny requests: their latency variance increased. Jain's index dropped in mixed-tenancy runs for fixed prefill policies. Introducing soft-differentiation (cap prefill participation ratio per tenant) substantially improved fairness at ~2% throughput cost.

Debug traces that helped pinpoint the issue:
- Microtraces captured in run #2026-01-22-incident-replay: trace shows a prefill batch formed at T=0 containing one 1024-token generation request and five tiny requests. The long request consumed ~120ms kernel time; all tiny requests stayed queued (head-of-line) for the same duration — explaining observed p99 spike.
- Heap of scheduler logs showed the prefill decision was purely slot-count based and unaware of in-flight length polymorphism.

Mitigations implemented in prod (quick fixes deployed 2026-01-25):
- Introduced soft-cap on prefill participation for requests with estimated generation length < 16 tokens. (Hotfix: pr/runtime#4123)
- Lowered default fixed prefill to 0.12 across mixed-tenant pools and added logging when prefill waits > 12ms.
- Short term rollback path: auto-fall back to timeout-only policy under queue-age jitter > 20ms in 1s window.

Longer-term proposals (next quarter):
- Request-length-aware prefill: integrate model hint (estimated tokens to generate) to avoid pinning tiny requests with long inflight ones. Prototype already in branch feature/prefill-by-estimate.
- Adaptive soft-deadlines: use per-request soft-deadline (based on SLA tier) and prefer forming batches that respect the tightest deadline in the candidate set. Could be integrated with rollout policies per customer tier.
- Tenant-aware prefill quotas: enforce per-tenant max participation fraction in prefill batches to guarantee fairness when loads spike.
- Improved simulator: extend our synthetic workload generator to model correlated microbursts (bursts with size and tenant correlations) and verify dynamic prefill heuristics under stress.

Action items (owners + tentative ETA):
- Merge request-length-estimate heuristics into canary (Jinwoo) — ETA 2026-03-12
- Implement per-tenant prefill quota enforcement and test in staging (Miguel) — ETA 2026-03-25
- Extend simulator to cover correlated microbursts and validate hybrid policy (Lena) — ETA 2026-04-01
- Postmortem writeup for infra/cs stakeholders summarizing impact on SLA and billing (Aisha) — ETA 2026-03-10

Open questions and unknowns:
- How accurate are model-provided length estimates across the model zoo we serve? Quantify false negatives where long requests are misclassified as short and slip into prefill sets.
- Is there an operational cost threshold where prefill complexity (dynamic heuristics, tenant quotas) outweighs gains for small customers? Need sizing analysis.
- Could KV-cache warm-up be decoupled from batch formation (i.e., speculative warm-up tasks) to avoid pinning slots? This may reduce latency coupling but introduces cost of extra GPU scheduling.

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Try a tiny microbenchmark that splits kernel submission into "warm-only" and "gen-only" passes and measure overhead. If overhead < 6% it might be ok to speculatively warm without holding consumer slots.
- Consider a simple rule-of-thumb: if predicted heavy-request probability within candidate set > 0.15 then prefer timeout-based flush for that window. Tune threshold in sim.

- Jupyter notebooks and synthetic workload configs are in the linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4123 (includes replay script run_replay.py and trace annotator).
- Raw CSV of metrics for runs referenced above: s3://redwood-experiments/2026/prefill-vs-timeout/ (internal access).
